title: Co-ordinated Sciences — DP Entrance
subject: science
instructions:
Answer **all** questions.

- Write your answer to each question in the space provided.
- You may use a calculator.
- You should show all your working and use appropriate units.
- Take the weight of 1.0 kg to be 9.8 N (acceleration of free fall = 9.8 m/s²).
- The total mark for this paper is 120. The number of marks for each question or part question is shown in brackets [ ].
- The Periodic Table is printed in the question paper.

questions.prompt:
A student investigates the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis in an aquatic plant. Fig. 1.1 shows the apparatus used. The student counts the number of bubbles of gas released in one minute.

Name the gas released by the aquatic plant.

A student investigates the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis in an aquatic plant. The student counts the number of bubbles of gas released in one minute and repeats the investigation with water at different temperatures. Table 1.1 shows the results.

**Table 1.1**

| temperature / °C | number of bubbles released per minute |
|---|---|
| 25 | 5 |
| 30 | 25 |
| 35 | 38 |
| 40 | 55 |
| 45 | 71 |
| 50 | 40 |
| 55 | 25 |
| 60 | 0 |

Describe the results shown in Table 1.1. Include data from Table 1.1 in your answer.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: correct description of the trend — the number of bubbles increases with temperature up to 45 °C, then decreases and reaches 0 at 60 °C.
1 mark: uses data from the table (e.g. quotes the peak of 71 bubbles per minute at 45 °C, or 0 bubbles at 60 °C).

questions.prompt:
In the photosynthesis investigation (Table 1.1), the number of bubbles released per minute was 40 at 50 °C, 25 at 55 °C and 0 at 60 °C.

Photosynthesis is an enzyme-controlled reaction.

Explain the results between 50 and 60 °C.
questions.criteria: Award up to 3 marks for: enzymes are denatured at high temperature; the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits / enzyme stops working; therefore the rate of photosynthesis decreases and stops (0 bubbles) at 60 °C.

questions.prompt:
The leaves of a plant are described as sources or as sinks depending on the time of the year.

Describe the difference between sources and sinks.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: a source is a part of the plant that releases/supplies sucrose (or amino acids) into the phloem for translocation.
1 mark: a sink is a part of the plant that receives/uses/stores sucrose (or amino acids) from the phloem.

questions.prompt: State the name of the carbohydrate in plants that is used **as an energy store**.
State the name of the carbohydrate in plants that is used **in respiration**.
State the name of the carbohydrate in plants that is used **to build cell walls**.

Measles is a transmissible disease. Fig. 2.1 shows the number of measles antibodies in the blood after vaccination and after infection.

Complete the sentence to explain the immune response seen in Fig. 2.1:

"Vaccinations contain a weakened form of the ______ or their antigens."

Complete the sentence about the immune response after vaccination (Fig. 2.1):

"The antigens stimulate an immune response by a type of white blood cell called ______."

Complete the sentence about the immune response after vaccination (Fig. 2.1):

"These white blood cells produce antibodies, increasing the number of antibodies in the blood. Long-term immunity is provided by the production of ______ cells."

Complete the sentence about the immune response seen in Fig. 2.1:

"If the body becomes infected after vaccination, antibody production in the body ______."
questions.answerKey: increases (faster and to a higher level than after vaccination)

questions.prompt:
Complete the sentence about the immune response seen in Fig. 2.1:

"The antibodies bind to antigens with a ______ shape destroying them or marking them for destruction."

Complete the sentence about the immune response seen in Fig. 2.1:

"The antibodies bind to antigens with a complementary shape destroying them or marking them for destruction by ______."
State the name of the type of immunity gained in Fig. 2.1 (immunity gained after vaccination).
State **two** indirect ways that transmissible diseases can be transmitted.
questions.criteria: 1 mark for each correct indirect method, any two of: via contaminated food or drink/water; from contaminated surfaces/objects; via the air/droplets/aerosols; via animals/vectors.

questions.prompt:
A country introduced a law called the Endangered Species Act. It was hoped that the Act would help to conserve species that were at risk from extinction. Table 3.1 shows the numbers of birds from different species before and after the Act was introduced.

**Table 3.1**

| species | number of birds before the Act | number of birds after the Act |
|---|---|---|
| bald eagle | 416 | 9789 |
| Kirtland's warbler | 210 | 1415 |
| nene goose | 400 | 1275 |
| peregrine falcon | 324 | 1700 |
| whooping crane | 54 | 513 |

State which species was the most at risk from extinction before the Act.

Using Table 3.1 (Kirtland's warbler: 210 birds before the Act, 1415 after the Act), calculate the percentage increase in the number of Kirtland's warblers.

Give your answer to the nearest whole number. Show your working.
List **three** reasons why species become endangered or extinct.
questions.criteria: 1 mark for each valid reason, any three of: climate change; habitat destruction/loss; hunting/over-harvesting; pollution; introduced/invasive species; disease; lack of food/competition.

questions.prompt:
The nene goose is a herbivore and the bald eagle is a carnivore.

State the name of the trophic level in the food chain for the nene goose.

The nene goose is a herbivore and the bald eagle is a carnivore.

Explain why the way the nene goose feeds is more energy efficient than that of the bald eagle.
questions.criteria: Award up to 3 marks for: the nene goose feeds at a lower trophic level / closer to the producer; energy is lost at each trophic level (e.g. as heat, in respiration, movement, undigested waste); so less energy has been lost from the food chain by the time the goose feeds / more of the original energy is available to it than to the bald eagle which feeds at a higher trophic level.

questions.prompt:
A student investigates the effect of exercise on oxygen consumption. The oxygen used by the student before, during and after exercise is monitored. Fig. 4.1 is a graph of the results.

State the balanced symbol equation for the type of respiration occurring **before exercise** in Fig. 4.1.
Use Fig. 4.1 to calculate the time taken by the student to exercise. Give your answer in minutes.

The shaded part of the graph in Fig. 4.1 represents an oxygen debt caused by a build-up of lactic acid.

State the **two** places where lactic acid builds up in the body during vigorous exercise.
Describe how the lactic acid is removed by the body after exercise.
questions.criteria: Award up to 3 marks for: continued fast/deep breathing supplies extra oxygen after exercise (repaying the oxygen debt); lactic acid is transported in the blood to the liver; in the liver lactic acid is oxidised / broken down (aerobically) to carbon dioxide and water.

questions.prompt:
Regular exercise reduces the risk of developing coronary heart disease (CHD).

Describe **one** change to a person's diet that can reduce the risk of developing CHD.
questions.criteria: 1 mark for one valid dietary change, e.g. eat less (saturated) fat/cholesterol; reduce salt intake; reduce sugar intake / eat fewer calories; eat more fruit and vegetables/fibre.

questions.prompt:
Fig. 5.1 shows the arrangement of the particles in the three states of matter. Table 5.1 shows information about the particles in the three states of matter.

**Table 5.1**

| state of matter | particle separation | particle arrangement | particle motion |
|---|---|---|---|
| solid | **(1) ______** | regular | vibrate about fixed positions |
| liquid | close together | (2) ______ | move around each other |
| gas | far apart | random | (3) ______ |

Complete gap **(1)**: state the particle separation for a **solid**.

Complete gap **(2)** in Table 5.1: state the particle arrangement for a **liquid**.

| state of matter | particle separation | particle arrangement | particle motion |
|---|---|---|---|
| solid | close together | regular | vibrate about fixed positions |
| liquid | close together | **(2) ______** | move around each other |
| gas | far apart | random | (3) ______ |

Complete gap **(3)** in Table 5.1: state the particle motion for a **gas**.

| state of matter | particle separation | particle arrangement | particle motion |
|---|---|---|---|
| solid | close together | regular | vibrate about fixed positions |
| liquid | close together | random | move around each other |
| gas | far apart | random | **(3) ______** |

Fig. 5.2 shows a cooling curve for water.

Write a letter **G** on Fig. 5.2 to show when the water is a gas and is cooling down.

[If you cannot draw on the figure, describe in words where the letter G should be placed.]
questions.criteria: 1 mark: G placed (or described) on the first steep downward-sloping section of the curve, before the first (higher) horizontal plateau — i.e. the top-left part of the graph.

questions.prompt:
Write a letter **F** on Fig. 5.2 to show when the water is freezing.

[If you cannot draw on the figure, describe in words where the letter F should be placed.]
questions.criteria: 1 mark: F placed (or described) on the second (lower) horizontal plateau of the cooling curve, where temperature stays constant while the liquid turns to solid.

questions.prompt: Explain how Fig. 5.2 (the cooling curve) shows that the water is pure rather than a mixture.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: the state changes happen at a constant/fixed temperature (flat, horizontal plateaus / sharp melting–freezing point); a mixture would change state over a range of temperatures.

questions.prompt:
While cooling, water vapour condenses to form liquid water.

Explain what happens to the particles when forming liquid water. Use ideas about the kinetic particle theory in your answer.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: particles lose (kinetic) energy and slow down / move more slowly.
1 mark: particles move closer together and attractive forces between them become significant / hold them close, so they can only move around each other.

questions.prompt:
Water is a simple molecular compound with a low melting point and a low boiling point.

Explain why the melting point and boiling point are low.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: there are weak intermolecular forces / weak forces of attraction between molecules.
1 mark: only a small amount of (heat) energy is needed to overcome these forces (the covalent bonds within molecules are not broken).

questions.prompt:
Aluminium is in Group III of the Periodic Table.

Give **one** reason why aluminium is often used in containers for food and drinks.
questions.criteria: 1 mark for one valid reason, e.g. resistant to corrosion (protective oxide layer) / unreactive with food; low density/lightweight; malleable/easily shaped; non-toxic.

questions.prompt:
Many metals react with dilute acids.

Complete the general equation for this reaction. Choose words from the list below:

alloy, base, hydrogen, oxygen, salt, water

metal + acid → ______ + ______

When aluminium metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, aluminium atoms form aluminium ions. The ionic half-equation for this reaction is shown:

Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻

State whether this reaction is oxidation or reduction. Explain your answer.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: oxidation, because the aluminium atom loses electrons (both the identification and the reason are needed).

questions.prompt:
Copper reacts with oxygen to form copper(II) oxide.

State whether copper(II) oxide is an acidic oxide or a basic oxide. Give a reason for your answer.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: basic oxide, because it is a metal oxide / it reacts with (neutralises) acids to form a salt and water (both the identification and a valid reason are needed).

questions.prompt:
Copper(II) oxide, CuO, reacts with sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate and water.

Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.

Fig. 6.1 shows the reaction pathway diagram for the reaction between copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid. In the diagram the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants.

State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: exothermic, because the products have less energy than the reactants / energy is released to the surroundings (both identification and reason needed).

questions.prompt: Define activation energy Eₐ.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: the minimum energy.
1 mark: that colliding particles/reactants must have for a reaction to occur / to start the reaction.

questions.prompt:
Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells use a chemical reaction to produce electricity.

Name the only chemical product made by a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

A vehicle with a petrol (gasoline) engine produces carbon dioxide gas. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.

Describe how carbon dioxide causes global warming.
questions.criteria: Award up to 3 marks for: (infrared/thermal) radiation is emitted from the Earth's surface; carbon dioxide absorbs this infrared radiation (preventing it escaping to space); the energy is re-emitted/trapped in the atmosphere so the temperature of the atmosphere/Earth rises.

questions.prompt:
Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells do **not** produce carbon dioxide.

Describe **one other** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells instead of petrol (gasoline) engines to power vehicles.
questions.criteria:
1 mark for a valid advantage, e.g. water is the only product / no toxic or polluting gases (CO, NOx, SO2) / hydrogen is renewable / quieter / more efficient.
1 mark for a valid disadvantage, e.g. hydrogen is difficult/dangerous to store or transport; few refuelling stations; producing hydrogen requires energy (often from fossil fuels); high cost.

questions.prompt:
A major component of petrol is the compound C₇H₁₆. C₇H₁₆ belongs to a homologous series.

Name the homologous series.

C₇H₁₆ burns in oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water:

C₇H₁₆ + 11O₂ → 7CO₂ + 8H₂O

Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide made when 2.5 g of C₇H₁₆ burns completely in oxygen. The molar gas volume at r.t.p. is 24 dm³. Show your working. Give your answer in dm³.

Magnesium chloride contains the ions Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻.

State the formula for magnesium chloride.

Magnesium chloride is a good conductor of electricity when aqueous. It does **not** conduct electricity when solid.

Explain why the conductivity of magnesium chloride is different in these two states.

- good conductor when aqueous: ...
- does **not** conduct electricity when solid: ...
questions.criteria:
1 mark: when aqueous, the ions are free to move (and carry charge/current).
1 mark: when solid, the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move.

questions.prompt:
Molten magnesium chloride can be electrolysed.

Construct the balanced ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.

Magnesium chloride is made when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.

A student reacts a piece of magnesium with 40 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid at 20 °C. The student measures the time taken for the reaction to finish. The student repeats the experiment at 30 °C and 40 °C.

Explain how increasing the temperature affects the rate of reaction.
questions.criteria: Award up to 4 marks for: rate of reaction increases; particles gain (kinetic) energy and move faster; there are more frequent collisions between particles; more of the colliding particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

questions.prompt:
The rate of reaction between magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid can be increased by adding a catalyst.

State how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (accept: it lowers the activation energy).

questions.prompt:
A car accelerates from rest with a **constant** acceleration of 10 m/s² for 3.0 seconds.

Define acceleration.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time (accept rate of change of velocity; accept a = Δv/t with symbols defined).

questions.prompt:
A car accelerates from rest with a **constant** acceleration of 10 m/s² for 3.0 seconds.

On Fig. 9.1, draw a speed–time graph for the car's motion.

[If you cannot draw on the grid, describe the graph you would draw in words, giving key coordinates.]
questions.criteria:
1 mark: a straight line starting at the origin (0, 0).
1 mark: correct constant gradient, ending at speed 30 m/s at time 3.0 s.

questions.prompt:
The mass of the car is 1750 kg.

Calculate the force required to produce an acceleration of 10 m/s². Give your answer in N.

Acceleration is a vector quantity.

State what is meant by the term *vector quantity*.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: a quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction.

questions.prompt:
Table 9.1 lists the quantities: acceleration, distance, energy, gravitational field strength, mass, velocity. Acceleration has already been identified as a vector.

From the remaining quantities (distance, energy, gravitational field strength, mass, velocity), state the **two** quantities that are vectors.

Two lamps are connected in parallel with a 12 V battery. The lamps are identical. Fig. 9.2 shows the circuit diagram for the lamps.

The current in the battery is 0.60 A.

Calculate the resistance of **one** of the lamps. State the unit for your answer.

Each headlamp of the car contains a thin converging lens. A converging lens can be used to form a virtual image.

Complete Fig. 9.3 to show how a converging lens forms a virtual image. (F = principal focus; the object is between the lens and F.)

[If you cannot draw on the figure, describe the rays you would draw and where the image forms.]
questions.criteria:
1 mark: a ray from the top of the object parallel to the axis, refracted through F on the far side of the lens.
1 mark: a ray from the top of the object passing straight through the centre of the lens; both rays extended backwards (dashed) on the object side.
1 mark: virtual image drawn/described where the backward extensions meet — on the same side as the object, upright and enlarged.

questions.prompt:
Fig. 10.1 shows a simple diagram of the Solar System. Saturn is in orbit around the Sun.

Draw an arrow (→) on Fig. 10.1 to show the direction of the force that keeps Saturn in orbit around the Sun.

[If you cannot draw on the figure, describe in words the direction of the arrow.]
questions.criteria: 1 mark: arrow drawn (or described) starting at Saturn and pointing directly towards the Sun (centripetal direction, towards the centre of the orbit).

questions.prompt: State the name of the force that keeps Saturn in orbit around the Sun.

The mean distance between Saturn and the Sun is 1.43 × 10¹² m. It takes 11 000 Earth days for Saturn to complete one orbit of the Sun.

Calculate the orbital speed of Saturn. Give your answer in m/s. Show your working.

The Sun is a stable star formed 5 billion years ago.

Describe the formation of a stable star.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: a cloud of gas (hydrogen) and dust (nebula) collapses/is pulled together by gravity, forming a protostar that heats up until nuclear fusion starts.
1 mark: the star becomes stable because the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from fusion/radiation (thermal expansion).

questions.prompt: Describe what the Big Bang Theory states in terms of the formation of the Universe.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: the whole Universe (all its matter/energy) was initially contained in a single, extremely small, hot and dense point/region.
1 mark: it expanded (in a giant 'explosion') about 14 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.

questions.prompt:
Fig. 11.1 shows a set of traffic lights containing light-emitting diodes (LEDs) coloured red, amber (orange) and green. The different coloured LEDs emit light with different frequencies and wavelengths.

Table 11.1 contains the frequencies and wavelengths of red, amber (orange) and green light. The amber (orange) LED has frequency 4.92 × 10¹⁴ Hz and wavelength 6.10 × 10⁻⁷ m (already identified).

**Table 11.1**

| | values |
|---|---|
| frequency / Hz | 4.62 × 10¹⁴, 4.92 × 10¹⁴ (amber), 5.66 × 10¹⁴ |
| wavelength / m | 5.30 × 10⁻⁷, 6.10 × 10⁻⁷ (amber), 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ |

Identify the frequency **and** the wavelength of the **red** LED.
Use the data in Table 11.1 for the amber (orange) LED (frequency 4.92 × 10¹⁴ Hz, wavelength 6.10 × 10⁻⁷ m) to show that the speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: uses v = f × λ, i.e. 4.92 × 10¹⁴ × 6.10 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (working shown).

questions.prompt:
Each LED has a potential difference of 3.6 V across it and a current of 0.025 A in it.

Calculate the total power input for each LED. Give your answer in W.

The LEDs have an efficiency of 40%.

Calculate the useful power output for each LED (total power input = 0.09 W). Give your answer in W.

Draw the circuit symbol for an LED.

[If you cannot draw, describe the symbol in words.]
questions.criteria: 1 mark: diode symbol (triangle pointing to a bar) inside/with a circle, with two small arrows pointing away from it (indicating emitted light).

questions.prompt:
Fig. 12.1 shows a diagram of a nuclear power station. The nuclear power station uses nuclear fission of uranium to generate electricity.

State what is meant by *nuclear fission*.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: the splitting of a large/heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei (releasing energy).

questions.prompt:
Thermal energy from the nuclear fission of uranium changes water into steam in the boiler.

Describe how the steam exerts a pressure inside the boiler.
questions.criteria:
1 mark: steam particles/molecules move (fast and randomly) and collide with the walls of the boiler.
1 mark: each collision exerts a force on the wall; the total force per unit area of the walls is the pressure.

questions.prompt:
The pressure in the steam causes the turbine to move faster.

State the type of energy store that increases when the turbine moves faster.

Fig. 12.2 shows a simple a.c. generator similar to the generator found in the power station. A magnetic field exists between the permanent magnets.

State what is meant by a *magnetic field*.
questions.criteria: 1 mark: a region (of space) in which a magnetic pole / magnetic material / magnet experiences a force.

questions.prompt:
One way of increasing the output e.m.f. of the generator is to rotate the coil faster.

State **two other** ways of increasing the output e.m.f. of the generator.
questions.criteria: 1 mark each, any two of: increase the number of turns on the coil; use stronger (permanent) magnets / stronger magnetic field; wind the coil on a soft-iron core; increase the area of the coil.

questions.prompt:
Fig. 12.3 shows the output e.m.f. from the generator.

On Fig. 12.3, sketch the output e.m.f. from the generator when the coil rotates faster.

[If you cannot draw on the figure, describe how the new curve differs from the original.]
questions.criteria:
1 mark: sketch/description shows a larger amplitude (higher peaks and deeper troughs) than the original.
1 mark: shows a shorter period / more cycles in the same time (higher frequency).
1 mark: wave remains a smooth a.c. sine shape alternating about zero.

importNotes: q52 (9(a)(ii)) uses the full page render page-20.png for the graph grid because the auto-cropped figures/p20-fig1.png lost its axis labels; the page render shows surrounding question text — a teacher may want a cleaner crop.

7 drawing/sketch tasks (5(b)(i), 5(b)(ii), 9(a)(ii), 9(d), 10(a)(i), 11(c), 12(b)(iii)) are paperOnly with describe-in-words fallbacks; teacher should decide whether typed descriptions are acceptable for credit.
Verbal answerKeys such as q60 '9500 (accept 9450–9500...)' and q56 '40 Ω (ohms)' rely on AI near-miss checking rather than exact match; teacher may want to normalise them to bare numbers.
Multi-blank parts were split into separate 1-point questions to allow auto-marking: 1(d) into 3, 2(a) cloze into 6 gaps, 5(a) table into 3; printed bracket totals are preserved exactly.

9(b)(ii) tick-the-vectors table converted to a 2-point short_answer listing the two vector quantities (gravitational field strength, velocity); 11(a)(i) tick-table similarly converted to a 1-point short_answer stating the red LED's frequency and wavelength.
6(b) word-choice equation completion (metal + acid → salt + hydrogen) modeled as a single 2-point short_answer with key 'salt and hydrogen' (either order acceptable).
Seven drawing/annotation tasks are paperOnly with a bracketed describe-in-words fallback: 5(b)(i), 5(b)(ii), 9(a)(ii), 9(d), 10(a)(i), 11(c), 12(b)(iii).

Some auto-cropped figures clip edge labels: figures/p04-fig1.png (Fig 2.1) loses part of the 'vaccination given' label, figures/p08-fig1.png (Fig 4.1) loses the y-axis caption; full page renders page-04.png / page-08.png can be substituted if clarity is an issue. page-20.png was used for Fig 9.1 because the crop lost its axis labels.
10(a)(iii) computed orbital speed is 9454 m/s; answer key set to 9500 with accepted range 9450–9500 noted in the key.
The original paper includes a Periodic Table (page 30) as a student reference; it is not attached to any question — consider providing page-30.png as a test-level reference.
